articles.title: It’s time to teach peer review as a core research skill
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03200-1Preprint journal clubs offer a scalable way to make peer-review training a routine part of scientific education.
articles.content:
Despite being a crucial part of science, peer review often isn’t included in university curricula.Credit: Getty

The rapidly growing volume of academic papers is outpacing the scientific community’s ability to critically evaluate them. This makes it increasingly important to equip the next generation of researchers with the skills that they need to become peer reviewers.

But formal curricula rarely include these skills. Universities invest years in teaching students how to design experiments and analyse data, but leave peer-review training mostly to informal mentorship.

So, how do early-career researchers — especially students and postdocs — learn to develop a critical eye?

Preprints offer a valuable opportunity for trainees to practise reviewing manuscripts outside the formal journal-review process, and several initiatives have been established with this in mind.

PREreview, for example, is a platform on which researchers can openly review and discuss preprints. And Preprint Club, a cross-institutional journal club run by an international group of universities, allows early-career researchers to select manuscripts for discussion so that they can learn from experience alongside their peers, more-senior researchers and faculty mentors.

Inspired by these efforts, we worked with the Bakar ImmunoX Initiative, a research programme at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), to launch our own preprint journal club, called ImmunoX Preprint JC, over the 2025–26 academic year.

We think that the journal club’s greatest value is in helping early-career researchers to build confidence and expertise in peer review. As a result, they are included in every level of conversation, from shaping how the club is run and how preprints are scored to leading discussions during journal-club sessions.

We also feel that other institutions could emulate this model, which combines hands-on experience, mentoring and relationship building, to support the development of their own early-career researchers.

Group discussion

Each monthly ImmunoX Preprint JC session follows the steps below. A postdoc starts by selecting an immunology-related preprint posted on the bioRxiv server. They choose an ImmunoX faculty ‘coach’, who helps them to assess the preprint on the basis of its scientific quality, impact and novelty. The manuscript and scoring rubric are shared with the wider ImmunoX community before the meeting.

At the meeting, the postdoc leads a 20-minute presentation discussing the preprint’s strengths and proposing experiments to improve it. Attendees then have a five- to ten-minute discussion about the preprint’s strengths and weaknesses; this is followed by anonymous scoring of the manuscript in terms of its scientific quality, impact and novelty.

Each manuscript’s publication status is tracked over several weeks to assess how well the ImmunoX community evaluated it. We plan to have the presenter of the top-scoring preprint over a six-month period write up a commentary with their coach. The piece would then be shared with the ImmunoX community and general public online.

Tracking progress

A key goal for the ImmunoX Preprint JC is to gauge whether the community-based assessment of a preprint reflects whether it is eventually accepted by a journal. Such data can establish a benchmark for how well our community — especially trainees — evaluates the scientific merits of a preprint.

We consulted with the Immunology Preprint Club at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City to compare scores given by both groups to the same preprints.

We also compared the preprints’ real-life performance with our scores. Although most of the preprints we have so far reviewed remain unpublished, our top-scoring paper was subsequently published in Cell1 — a leading life-sciences journal — suggesting that community-based assessments can, at least in some cases, identify work that will go on to meet the standards of a high-profile journal. Our findings from the 2025–26 academic year can be viewed in more detail on the ImmunoX website.

Assessing our own data allows us not only to track occasions we’ve correctly identified high-quality work, but also to pick up on potential biases. For example, we noticed that manuscripts whose senior authors were highly cited tended to receive higher scores in our journal-club sessions. This could mean that our community reliably identified rigorous science, or it might reflect an unconscious bias correlating reputation with scientific quality.

Learning to notice this will help trainees to develop more self-awareness, which is crucial for an unbiased peer-review process. In the future, we plan to withhold manuscript author names until the end of a scoring session.

articles.personality_title: New program teaches young scientists how to review research papers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Peer review is an important part of science where experts check each other's work to make sure it is correct and useful. However, universities usually do not teach students how to do peer review, leaving many young researchers unprepared.

**What happened** – A group at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) started a special journal club called ImmunoX Preprint JC during the 2025–26 school year. In this club, early-career researchers pick new scientific papers (called preprints) to review together. They discuss the paper’s strengths and weaknesses, score it, and get help from experienced scientists. The club also tracks how these papers do later, such as whether they get published in big journals.

**Impact** – This program helps young scientists learn how to carefully evaluate research, build confidence, and understand possible biases in reviewing. For example, they noticed that papers by famous scientists sometimes got higher scores, which shows the reviewers are learning to be aware of their own judgments. One highly rated paper was later published in a top journal, showing the club’s reviews can spot good science.

**What's next step** – The club plans to keep improving by hiding author names during scoring to reduce bias. They also want others to use this model to train more early-career researchers in peer review. Presenters of top papers will write commentaries to share their insights more widely.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new journal club at UCSF is teaching young scientists how to review research papers, helping them gain important skills and improve the quality of scientific evaluation.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau programme apprend aux jeunes scientifiques à évaluer les recherches
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La revue par les pairs est une étape essentielle en science où des experts vérifient le travail des autres pour s'assurer qu'il est correct et utile. Pourtant, les universités n'enseignent généralement pas cette compétence, laissant de nombreux jeunes chercheurs sans préparation.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Un groupe de l'Université de Californie à San Francisco (UCSF) a lancé un club de revue appelé ImmunoX Preprint JC durant l'année scolaire 2025–26. Dans ce club, de jeunes chercheurs choisissent ensemble des articles scientifiques récents (appelés prépublications) à évaluer. Ils discutent des points forts et des faiblesses, attribuent des notes et sont aidés par des scientifiques expérimentés. Le club suit aussi la suite donnée à ces articles, comme leur publication dans des grandes revues.

**Impact** – Ce programme aide les jeunes scientifiques à apprendre à analyser les recherches avec soin, à gagner en confiance et à reconnaître leurs propres biais. Par exemple, ils ont remarqué que les articles d'auteurs célèbres recevaient parfois de meilleures notes, ce qui montre qu'ils prennent conscience de leurs jugements. Un article très bien noté a ensuite été publié dans une revue prestigieuse, prouvant que les évaluations du club repèrent la bonne science.

**Prochaine étape** – Le club prévoit de cacher les noms des auteurs lors des évaluations pour réduire les biais. Ils souhaitent aussi que d'autres institutions adoptent ce modèle pour former plus de jeunes chercheurs à la revue par les pairs. Les présentateurs des meilleurs articles écriront des commentaires pour partager leurs idées plus largement.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un nouveau club de revue à l'UCSF enseigne aux jeunes scientifiques à évaluer des articles de recherche, leur permettant d'acquérir des compétences clés et d'améliorer la qualité de l'évaluation scientifique.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo programa enseña a jóvenes científicos a revisar investigaciones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La revisión por pares es una parte importante de la ciencia donde expertos revisan el trabajo de otros para asegurarse de que sea correcto y útil. Sin embargo, las universidades generalmente no enseñan esta habilidad, dejando a muchos jóvenes investigadores sin preparación.

**Qué pasó** – Un grupo en la Universidad de California en San Francisco (UCSF) inició un club especial llamado ImmunoX Preprint JC durante el año escolar 2025–26. En este club, investigadores jóvenes eligen juntos nuevos artículos científicos (llamados preprints) para revisar. Discuten las fortalezas y debilidades, los califican y reciben ayuda de científicos con experiencia. El club también sigue qué pasa con esos artículos después, como si se publican en revistas importantes.

**Impacto** – Este programa ayuda a los jóvenes científicos a aprender a evaluar la investigación con cuidado, ganar confianza y entender posibles prejuicios en la revisión. Por ejemplo, notaron que los artículos de científicos famosos a veces recibían mejores calificaciones, lo que muestra que los revisores están aprendiendo a ser conscientes de sus propios juicios. Un artículo muy bien calificado fue publicado después en una revista importante, mostrando que las revisiones del club pueden identificar buena ciencia.

**Próximo paso** – El club planea mejorar ocultando los nombres de los autores durante la calificación para reducir prejuicios. También quieren que otros usen este modelo para formar a más jóvenes investigadores en revisión por pares. Los presentadores de los mejores artículos escribirán comentarios para compartir sus ideas más ampliamente.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un nuevo club de revista en UCSF enseña a jóvenes científicos a revisar artículos de investigación, ayudándoles a ganar habilidades importantes y mejorar la calidad de la evaluación científica.

articles.title: The surprising history of pumpkins: from ancient staple to autumn icon
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Pumpkin spice lattes, jack-o’-lanterns, and Thanksgiving pies: pumpkins are the unofficial mascots of fall. But behind their seasonal charm lies a deeper, more complicated story that winds through language, history, agriculture, and even a little insult comedy. “Pumpkins are more popular than ever,” says Cindy Ott, associate professor of […]
The post The surprising history of pumpkins: from ancient staple to autumn icon first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Pumpkin spice lattes, jack-o’-lanterns, and Thanksgiving pies: pumpkins are the unofficial mascots of fall. But behind their seasonal charm lies a deeper, more complicated story that winds through language, history, agriculture, and even a little insult comedy.

“Pumpkins are more popular than ever,” says Cindy Ott, associate professor of history at the University of Delaware and author of Pumpkin: The Curious History of an American Icon. But our obsession with this humble gourd, she notes, is tied less to flavor and more to a nostalgic longing for simpler, rural times. “People are buying these things, even pumpkin spice lattes, because of these attachments, these very old-fashioned ideas about reverence of the small family farm.”

A name with roots that twist like a vine

The word “pumpkin” has always been more conceptual than botanical. According to Logan Kistler, curator of archaeobotany at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, the term refers to squash varieties bred to resemble the round, orange gourds we associate with fall. “Pumpkin isn’t exactly a botanical group,” he explains.

Linguistically, the word has had quite a journey. Fiona McPherson of the Oxford English Dictionary traces it from the Greek pepon to the French pompon, which eventually morphed into the English “pompion” in the 1500s. “Pumpkin,” as we know it today, first appeared in print in 1647, ironically in reference to the meager diet of early settlers.

But while the word took a European path, the plant itself is deeply American. Indigenous peoples across North, Central, and South America cultivated early pumpkin ancestors, domesticating different types of Cucurbita as far back as 10,000 years ago in Mexico. “Pumpkins are part of this genus Cucurbita,” says Kistler, noting that they were farmed widely throughout the Americas long before colonists arrived.

From insult to endearment

Surprisingly, it didn’t take long for the word “pumpkin” to go from dietary staple to verbal jab. By the late 1600s, it was being used as an insult.

“It really did not take long for it to develop this figurative use,” says McPherson. Pumpkin became a shorthand for someone who was conceited, dim-witted, or full of hot air.

Cindy Ott adds that gender played a role in the insult’s direction. For women, pumpkin imagery was linked to the body and “natural urges,” seen as a lack of refinement. For men, it implied an empty head. “It’s been used for politicians for hundreds of years,” she notes.

A symbol of imagined agrarian purity

By the late 19th century, the pumpkin was undergoing a cultural rehabilitation. It shifted from insult to affection, and from staple crop to nostalgic icon.

“So Americans move out of the country, into the city, but they like to imagine themselves farmers at heart, many of them,” Ott explains. As industrialization transformed the U.S., the pumpkin came to symbolize the pastoral life being left behind. In poetry, paintings, and festivals, it became a stand-in for tradition and a romanticized vision of national roots.

Today, that symbolism is being put to work, literally. Pumpkins are once again supporting small farmers, not as dietary staples but as attractions. Ott calls them “agrarian wonderlands,” where farms market autumnal experiences that hinge on the iconic gourd.

“The cool thing about the whole story,” Ott says, “is that these very romantic ideas and myths that a lot of Americans tell themselves about their origin stories are actually helping to rejuvenate the very thing it represents: a small family farm.”

articles.personality_title: How pumpkins grew from ancient food to a symbol of fall and small farms
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Pumpkins are well known today for fall traditions like pumpkin spice lattes and Halloween pumpkins. But their story goes back thousands of years to when Native Americans first grew them as food.

**What happened** – The word “pumpkin” comes from old languages like Greek and French, changing over time before becoming common in English in the 1600s. Early settlers ate pumpkins as a basic food, but the word was soon used as an insult to mean someone silly or empty-headed. By the 1800s, as people moved to cities, pumpkins became a symbol of simpler rural life and family farming.

**Impact** – Today, pumpkins help small farms by attracting visitors to pumpkin patches and events, supporting local farmers. This shows how a simple plant can connect people to history, farming, and community in a way that helps farms thrive.

**What's next step** – Farms will likely keep using pumpkins as a way to bring people closer to farming life and support family farms. This could encourage more people to appreciate where their food comes from and help keep small farms alive.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Pumpkins have traveled from ancient crops to fall icons that now help small farms stay strong and connect communities to their roots.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment les citrouilles sont passées d’un aliment ancien à un symbole de l’automne et des petites fermes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Aujourd’hui, les citrouilles sont célèbres pour les traditions d’automne comme les lattes à la citrouille épicée et les citrouilles d’Halloween. Mais leur histoire remonte à des milliers d’années, lorsque les peuples autochtones d’Amérique les cultivaient comme nourriture.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le mot « citrouille » vient de langues anciennes comme le grec et le français, évoluant avant de devenir courant en anglais au 17e siècle. Les premiers colons mangeaient des citrouilles comme aliment de base, mais le mot a vite été utilisé comme insulte pour désigner quelqu’un de bête ou vide d’esprit. Au 19e siècle, alors que les gens quittaient la campagne pour la ville, la citrouille est devenue un symbole de la vie rurale simple et de la ferme familiale.

**Impact** – Aujourd’hui, les citrouilles aident les petites fermes en attirant des visiteurs dans les champs de citrouilles et lors d’événements, soutenant ainsi les agriculteurs locaux. Cela montre comment une plante simple peut relier les gens à l’histoire, à l’agriculture et à la communauté pour aider les fermes à prospérer.

**Prochaine étape** – Les fermes continueront probablement à utiliser les citrouilles pour rapprocher les gens de la vie agricole et soutenir les fermes familiales. Cela pourrait encourager plus de personnes à apprécier l’origine de leur nourriture et à aider à préserver les petites fermes.

**Phrase clé** – Les citrouilles sont passées de cultures anciennes à icônes de l’automne qui aident aujourd’hui les petites fermes à rester fortes et à connecter les communautés à leurs racines.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo las calabazas pasaron de alimento antiguo a símbolo del otoño y de las pequeñas granjas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hoy en día, las calabazas son famosas por tradiciones otoñales como los lattes con especias de calabaza y las calabazas de Halloween. Pero su historia se remonta a miles de años atrás, cuando los pueblos indígenas de América las cultivaban como alimento.

**Qué pasó** – La palabra “calabaza” viene de idiomas antiguos como el griego y el francés, cambiando con el tiempo antes de ser común en inglés en el siglo XVII. Los primeros colonos comían calabazas como alimento básico, pero la palabra pronto se usó como insulto para referirse a alguien tonto o sin cerebro. En el siglo XIX, cuando la gente se mudó del campo a la ciudad, la calabaza se volvió un símbolo de la vida rural sencilla y de la granja familiar.

**Impacto** – Hoy, las calabazas ayudan a las pequeñas granjas al atraer visitantes a los campos y eventos de calabazas, apoyando a los agricultores locales. Esto muestra cómo una planta sencilla puede conectar a las personas con la historia, la agricultura y la comunidad para ayudar a que las granjas prosperen.

**Próximo paso** – Probablemente, las granjas seguirán usando las calabazas para acercar a la gente a la vida agrícola y apoyar las granjas familiares. Esto podría animar a más personas a valorar de dónde viene su comida y ayudar a mantener vivas las pequeñas granjas.

**Frase clave** – Las calabazas han viajado desde cultivos antiguos hasta convertirse en iconos otoñales que ahora ayudan a las pequeñas granjas a mantenerse fuertes y a conectar a las comunidades con sus raíces.
